pages.x: Vietnam's emperors, followers of Confucius, saw Christianity as a threat, and had European missionaries and Vietnamese Catholics put to death. Napoleon III's France wanted a foothold in Asia to rival Britain. In September 1858 a French and Spanish fleet sailed into the bay of Tourane, now Da Nang, and took its forts.

Hemmed in at Tourane by Vietnamese troops and sickness, the French sailed south and in February 1859 took the citadel of Saigon, a rice port in the Mekong delta far from the capital, Hue. In 1861 they broke the Vietnamese siege lines at Ky Hoa and overran the country around.

Emperor Tu Duc was a scholar and poet who ruled from the citadel of Hue. Faced with a rebellion in the north as well, he signed the Treaty of Saigon in 1862, giving France three southern provinces, paying a heavy indemnity and letting missionaries preach. He hoped to buy the lost land back. He never could.

France made Cambodia a protectorate in 1863, and in 1867 seized the three western provinces of the delta. Their governor, the old mandarin Phan Thanh Gian, who had gone to Paris to beg for the lost lands back, had no means to fight. He handed over the forts to spare his people a massacre, then took poison. All the south was now the French colony of Cochinchina.

In the north, trade on the Red River drew French adventurers. In 1873 Francis Garnier, with a couple of hundred men, stormed the citadel of Hanoi. The court called on the Black Flags, Chinese irregulars under Liu Yongfu who had settled on the river, and they ambushed and killed Garnier outside Hanoi. France disowned him and pulled out.

In 1882 Commander Henri Rivière took Hanoi again, and in May 1883 he too was killed by the Black Flags, near the same spot. This time France sent a real army and fleet. In August 1883, with Tu Duc just dead, French warships shelled the forts guarding Hue, and the court signed a treaty that put Vietnam under French protection.

China, which saw Vietnam as its vassal, sent armies into the north alongside the Black Flags, and France and China went to war. On 23 August 1884 Admiral Courbet's squadron, which had lain at anchor for weeks beside the Chinese fleet in the river at Fuzhou, opened fire and sank it in under an hour.

On land the war went less well. In March 1885, after a defeat at Bang Bo, a French force in retreat abandoned the town of Lang Son. When the news reached Paris it caused a panic, and the prime minister who had pushed for the war, Jules Ferry, mocked as "the Tonkinese", was thrown out of office. Yet in June China signed away its claims.

In July 1885 the regent Ton That Thuyet attacked the French in Hue, failed, and fled into the mountains with the 13-year-old emperor Ham Nghi. In the boy's name he called on all Vietnamese to rise in the Can Vuong, Aid the King, movement. The French put another emperor on the throne and spent more than ten years crushing the revolt.

In 1887 France joined Vietnam's three regions and Cambodia, and later Laos, into French Indochina. Ham Nghi, captured in 1888, spent the rest of his life in exile in Algeria, where he became a painter. Vietnamese resistance never quite died, and in 1954, at Dien Bien Phu, France's rule came to an end.
pts: All of Vietnam was French by 1885
French rule ended at Dien Bien Phu in 1954
